li.a: Serial Killer Calendar: Paul Charles Denyer
ABC News: Frankston serial killer Paul Denyer denied parole three decades after murders
The Age: Frankston serial killer Paul Denyer denied parole
ABC News: Victorian government to introduce laws to keep Frankston serial killer Paul Denyer in prison for life
Tea True Crime: Issue 29, The Frankston Murders
Take 5: The Frankston serial killer murdered my mum

content.p: Paul Charles Denyer was 21 when he confessed, in the early hours of 1 August 1993, to the murders of three young women in Melbourne's south-east. He pleaded guilty and became known as the Frankston serial killer. Ten years into his sentence it emerged that he had begun to identify as a woman and call himself Paula, and the name was used in some media coverage; a request to change his name legally was refused. He was sentenced to three consecutive terms of life imprisonment. A Victorian court later fixed a minimum of 30 years, and the Adult Parole Board of Victoria turned down his 2023 application for release. Later that year the state government said it would introduce laws aimed at keeping him in prison for life.

According to one biographical account, Denyer was born on 14 April 1972 at Campbelltown, on the edge of Sydney, the third of six children of parents who had married in London and emigrated to Australia in 1965. They relocated to Victoria in 1981. School was hard for him, and he became very heavy in his teens. The same account says that as a ten-year-old he took a blade to his sister's teddy bear and killed the family cat, that he was cautioned over a stolen car before his thirteenth birthday and that at fifteen he was arrested after assaulting another student. It says he lost seven jobs after leaving school and did not pass the medical for Victoria Police.

He started work in February 1993 at a boat-building firm in Seaford, where colleagues noticed him making knives, and his employment ended a few months afterwards. That same month a young mother in Seaford returned home to find her unit wrecked, her cat dissected and her kittens drowned, with the words "Donna you're dead" written on the wall in blood. Denyer later admitted to that attack and said he would have killed her had she been at home, the same account reports. A newsletter retelling of the case adds that she had been out with her partner and baby that night and that the couple's pets were killed. Denyer told detectives after his arrest that he had been stalking women around Frankston "for years", that he had wanted to kill since he was 14 and that he hated girls and women in general. The Age reported that he had said he had been stalking hundreds of women since he was 17.

Elizabeth Stevens had come from Tasmania to enrol at the Frankston TAFE college, with hopes of an army career, and lived with relatives in Langwarrin. On the evening of Friday 11 June 1993 she stepped off a bus on Cranbourne Road and was grabbed as she turned into her street. According to the account on Serial Killer Calendar, heavy rain and wind covered her screams, and people who saw Denyer walking her down the street took them for a couple. She was killed in a nearby park, and a man gathering pine branches found her body the next day. Her age is given as 18 by the ABC, The Age and Casefile, and as 17 in the Take 5 magazine piece.

On 8 July Denyer attacked a woman walking home from Seaford station. She fought free and was picked up by a passing car. The ABC described her as a 41-year-old bank clerk, and Serial Killer Calendar says the gun held to her head was a fake.

That same evening Debbie Fream, 22 according to the ABC and The Age, left her 12-day-old son at home with a friend and went out for milk. The Age says she wanted eggs for an omelette; the ABC, Casefile and others say milk. Denyer later told police he had hidden in the back seat of her car while she was in a shop and ambushed her when she returned. A farmer found her body in a paddock at Carrum Downs four days later. Like Stevens, she had been strangled and her throat cut, the ABC reported. The baby, Jake Blair, grew up not knowing how his mother had died. In a Take 5 article he describes how, as a boy, his father took him to her grave in the town where both parents had grown up, and how he later read the old press coverage. Serial Killer Calendar says her car turned up the next day on a street in the area and that a canvass of 4,700 homes there, code-named Operation Pulsar, was the largest Victoria Police had mounted. Her death, linked with Stevens's, made clear that a serial killer was at large. Frankston, the Take 5 account says, became a ghost town, and local women were warned not to go out alone after dark.
content.h2: Natalie Russell and the track between the golf courses
content.p: Natalie Russell was a Year 12 student at John Paul College, 17 according to the ABC, The Age and Casefile. The school had given safety talks after the earlier attacks and told students not to use a shortcut between two golf courses, but students including Natalie still used it, a retelling of the case says. On Friday 30 July she left school early and took the track.

A postal worker on Skye Road in Frankston North had noticed a man in a rusty yellow Toyota Corona with no number plates, watching the track through binoculars, according to Serial Killer Calendar. She saw a schoolgirl approach and the man get out and follow her, and she called the police. Officers came, wrote down the car's registration, spoke to a few neighbours and were called to another job before the man came back. The ABC says police recorded the registration at the time. That evening Natalie was reported missing, and searchers found her body in the scrub beside the track. The ABC says she had been stabbed and strangled, and that police were able to recover crucial DNA evidence from her body. Serial Killer Calendar adds that three holes in the fence had been cut with one tool and that one of them carried blood. The path is now known as Nat's Track.
The ABC states that Russell was killed 18 days after Fream. Reports that give the dates of those two killings as 8 July and 30 July would put the gap at 22 days. The sources do not reconcile this.

The registration led detectives to Denyer, who lived with his girlfriend in a unit in Seaford. They visited the next afternoon. He told them he had been near the scenes of two of the murders and could not explain the cuts and scratches on his hands, and he agreed to give a DNA sample. The ABC says he suspected the test would prove his guilt. In the early hours of 1 August he admitted all three murders, a further attack and a run of burglaries. A podcast series by Vikki Petraitis, the crime writer who has written a book on the case and was on patrol with police the night of the last murder, describes the confession as boastful and says he spoke to detectives as though they were friends.

Denyer admitted three counts of murder and one of abduction. According to Serial Killer Calendar, psychologists found a sadistic personality disorder, not insanity, and he told examiners that the 1987 film The Stepfather had influenced him. The Take 5 article says the Supreme Court of Victoria heard that he had fantasised about killing women for three years.

On 20 December 1993, after four days of hearings, Justice Frank Vincent sentenced him to three consecutive life terms and declined to set a non-parole period. The ABC quotes him as describing the crimes as "almost beyond comprehension" and telling Denyer: "I suspect that you will never fully comprehend why this should be so as, for reasons which we do not understand, in an important sense you are not one of us." He noted that the disorder was probably untreatable and that Denyer had expressed no remorse. Public anger followed when the sentence was reduced on appeal. The ABC and The Age report that the Court of Appeal set a minimum of 30 years, which made him eligible to apply for parole in 2023. One newsletter says the appeal was to the High Court; the ABC and The Age name the Court of Appeal. The reduction was made in July 1994, according to Serial Killer Calendar.

Vincent later reflected, according to The Age, that beyond the victims and their families there were "many thousands of women and others who had to live with this fear". Jeff Kennett, premier of Victoria at the time, recalled to the same paper that there was outrage and "genuine, genuine fear".

Denyer was held at Barwon Prison and later at Port Phillip. Serial Killer Calendar says that in 2003 he began to identify as a woman and called himself Paula. In a letter to another inmate he wrote that he had committed the murders "not because I ever hated womankind, but because I have never really felt that I was male." Prison authorities refused him make-up and surgery, and a legal change of name was also refused. The ABC says the request for gender reassignment surgery, made about ten years into the sentence, was denied. The mother of one of the victims described the transition as a stunt, according to Serial Killer Calendar. By 2022, the same account says, he had gone back to using the name Paul.
content.h2: The 2023 parole bid and the law that followed
content.p: In May 2023 Brian Russell, Natalie's father, was told by the justice department that the parole board had dismissed the application. "We've been on tenterhooks for some time now, hoping that this would be the outcome," he told the ABC. He said he and his wife Carmel wanted the law changed so that Denyer could never apply again. Retired detective inspector Bernie Rankin, who had been stationed at Frankston in 1993, told The Age it was "just too great a risk to release him". The board said that confidentiality rules in the Corrections Act 1986 prevented it from commenting. Jake Blair joined the relatives of the victims in demanding that Denyer never be released.

David Limbrick, a member of the Victorian Parliament who had been Natalie Russell's boyfriend, renewed his push for legislation. In June 2023 the Liberal and National parties introduced a bill to keep Denyer in prison for life, which the Labor government voted down. Attorney-General Jaclyn Symes defended that decision, saying it was right to take time "to get the package right". On 31 October 2023 the government announced a broader bill that the ABC said was designed with the Russell family. It would let the parole board set a "no return" date for people serving life sentences or bar serial killers and child murderers from applying for up to ten years, and create a restricted-prisoner category. The ABC understood that the legislation named Denyer and would keep him from release unless he was physically incapacitated or terminally ill. Brian Russell welcomed the announcement. Greg Barns of the Australian Lawyers Alliance criticised the bill, arguing that courts, not governments, should set sentences and parole.

Frankston MP Paul Edbrooke said in 2023 that the community was still scared by the events of three decades earlier and that some people still checked the back of their cars before driving. The case has been the subject of a book and a podcast by Vikki Petraitis, and the podcast was released through Casefile Presents.
